articles.title: Muslims Are Projected to Become the World’s Largest Religious Group by 2035, Surpassing Christians. Here’s Why
articles.summary: Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group —overtaking Christians , who have long held that distinction—by 2035. And the gap between the two populations is set to keep steadily widening in the ensuing decades if recent trends continue, with Muslims potentially representing 3.64 billion people around the globe in 2070 compared to 2.96 billion Christians. articles.title: Scientists Are Pursuing the Dream of a 'Virtual Cell'
articles.summary: A single cell is a world unto itself, billions of interlocking molecules whose intricate patterns foretell health and disease. Biologists usually investigate how cells work in the lab. But in recent years, the idea of a “virtual cell” —a computer model so detailed, with such a close resemblance to the real thing, that scientists could run experiments on it instead of in the lab—has entered the conversation . articles.title: In Elsinore, a Radiant Andrew Scott Finds Life in a Play About Death
articles.summary: Contracting HIV is no longer a death sentence. But before the current medications and treatments emerged, the AIDS crisis of the 1980s and 1990s touched almost everyone, gay or straight, whether you wanted to admit it or not. Friends of friends, acquaintances or associates who brightened your day, or, worst of all, a loved one: people you cherished could wither and disappear in practically a heartbeat. articles.title: Elsinore and the Remarkable True Story of a Dying Actor’s Triumph as Hamlet
articles.summary: On the evening of Nov. 13, 1989, Ian Charleson walked onto the Olivier stage at London’s National Theatre to play Hamlet for the last time. He was 40 years old and dying of AIDS, though few of the 1,150 or so people watching from the dark knew it. The illness had puffed the skin around his eyes and affected his throat and chest, but the change in his face had been explained away as sinus surgery. articles.title: A Black Figure Skater Just Made History. Here’s Why It Matters
articles.summary: Last weekend, American figure skater Alexa Gasparotto made history as the first Black woman ever to land a triple axel at the International Skating Union Grand Prix. This jump is symbolic of something far larger. While Black competitors in Olympic figure skating are still few and far between, we exist vibrantly. Gasparotto’s triple axel was a byproduct of a long effort in a small, expensive sport for more visibility and support for skaters of all marginalized backgrounds.
